title: The NFL’s Salute to Service honors the military – and leaves out the realities of war | Lee Escobedo
text:
My mom taught me to thank veterans. Whenever we saw someone in a veterans hat, she set the example. Nobody in her family served, but my paternal grandfather fought in the Pacific in the second world war, and she was always grateful to hear his stories, even the repeats.
It’s one of the things she gave me that I held on to, even in my worst years. The anger I’ve carried about the unjust wars of my lifetime – Afghanistan, Iraq and now Iran – never targeted the people sent to fight them.
So when the NFL spends November saluting service, I’m exactly the fan it has in mind. I stand for the anthem, proudly. On Veterans Day, representatives of the NFL’s five Salute to Service charities rang the Nasdaq opening bell. On 21 November, NBC will air an hour-long Salute to Service special. Every team plays a game with camouflage stencils on the field, while Nike, New Era, Wilson and Riddell sell you the matching gear.
But I can’t tolerate what the league leaves out. This is the 16th Salute to Service and the first since the United States and Israel went to war with Iran in February. The Pentagon’s casualty system counts 23 American service members killed and 865 wounded, and that’s before we get to the thousands of Iranians who have lost their lives, including schoolchildren. In a recent interview Donald Trump was vague about the number of US military deaths in Iran.
Like Trump, the league is keen to be associated with the military without getting into the specifics. The league’s announcement for this year’s Salute to Service runs well past 1,000 words. The word Iran doesn’t appear in it. It won’t say where those service members are serving, or what the war has cost them.
That’s because when the NFL says it honors service, it mostly means the spectacle of service, with a charitable line item attached. The league says Salute to Service has raised more than $80m since 2011, a little more than $5m a year. That sounds a lot – and the league does contribute to very worthwhile veterans charities – but consider that NFL commissioner, Roger Goodell, alone reportedly earned $63.9m in the 2020 season, the last time the league was obliged to disclose his salary. Or that league revenue in 2025 was estimated to be $23bn.
What we don’t hear about among the flag waving and flyovers during Salute to Service is what’s killing veterans. The Department of Veterans Affairs’ annual suicide report counted 6,488 veteran taking their own lives in 2024, nearly 18 a day. Disturbingly, 62% of those veterans hadn’t received VA health care in the year before they died, and a gun was used in 74.3% of the deaths.
The Department of Housing and Urban Development’s January 2025 count found 32,495 veterans homeless on any given night, a record low, down more than half since 2010. Federal money for housing vouchers and landlord outreach impacted that. Not flyovers. A league with $23bn in revenue could move that number in the right direction. The federal government of the richest country in the world could do even more.
Then there’s the war the NFL won’t name. A new cohort of wounded Americans is coming home from a war that I believe the United States is fighting at least partly on Israel’s behalf and without a purpose that anyone in Washington can state honestly. In July, the Defense Department cut the number of troops listed as killed in Operation Epic Fury from 18 to 14, while new casualties appeared under a heading called Overseas Operations. In October, after the Washington Post found more dead than the department was disclosing, the Pentagon raised its count to 21. It stands at 23 as I write this.
The NFL would argue that it is a sports league, and that it is the government’s job to support veterans. That argument holds water, but by associating itself so closely to veterans – and by benefiting from that association in a country where the public holds the armed forces in high esteem – the league also needs to give back.
The NFL could start by mentioning the war with Iran. Put the 23 names of slain soldiers on the screen at games, and say where and how they died. Have Goodell say, out loud, that a league honoring service wants the people doing the serving to come home, and that the men and women on the bases in Jordan and Qatar aren’t the ones who decided to send them there. That decision belongs to the Trump administration. Nothing in that statement is hostile to the military.
On the money, tie the commitment to revenue and publish the number. A 10th of 1% of what the clubs took in last year would be about $23m, more than four times what Salute to Service raises now. Aim where the data points: at housing; at outreach to the 62% of veterans who die without ever touching the VA; at safe firearm storage; and at brain injury and post-traumatic stress care, where the NFL, after its own concussion reckoning, has hard-won expertise.
Some of what the league funds now is good. The Tragedy Assistance Program for Survivors does real grief work, and the USA Wheelchair Football League exists because the Bob Woodruff Foundation and the NFL built it. But the NFL’s announcement names five partners and omits the annual dollar figure.
A country this rich shouldn’t need a sports league to look after its veterans, and the 32,495 homeless veterans are a federal failure before they’re anyone else’s. But nobody made the NFL do this. It painted the camouflage on its own fields and put the words Salute to Service on a Nasdaq bell. When the NBC special airs on 21 November, the Pentagon’s death toll may have moved again, and nobody on the broadcast will have the patriotism to mention it.
